questions.question: Select the sentence in which the '-ing' form of verb expresses the continuity of an action/event.
questions.questionHtml: Select the sentence in which the '-ing' form of verb expresses the continuity of an action/event.

options.text: Writing poetry is a relaxing activity.
options.html: Writing poetry is a relaxing activity.

options.text: I have a career in writing.
options.html: I have a career in writing.

options.text: The students are discussing the project details.
options.html: The students are discussing the project details.

options.text: He bought a writing pad for his notes.
options.html: He bought a writing pad for his notes.

questions.solution:
Option (c): The '-ing' form of the verb "discussing" in this sentence is part of the present continuous tense ("are discussing"), which indicates that the action is happening now and expresses the continuity of the event.

Option (a): Here, the '-ing' form "writing" is a gerund, which functions as a noun and does not express the continuity of an action/event while the '-ing' form "relaxing" is an adjective modifying the noun 'activity'.

Option (b): Here also, the '-ing' form "writing" is a gerund, which functions as a noun and does not express the continuity of an action/event.

Option (d): The '-ing' form "writing" here is an adjective describing the type of pad. It does not indicate the continuity of any action/event.

Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

Note:

Gerund: Gerund is a verb form that functions as a noun, ending in -ing. A gerund can be either the subject or object of a sentence in English. Example: "Everybody enjoyed her dancing and singing at the party." The words 'dancing' and 'singing' are gerunds.

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options. A. The photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during an our vacation in the Maldives. B. A photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives. C. An photo captured the beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in a Maldives. D. The photo captured a beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the grammatically correct statement from among the given options.

A. The photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during an our vacation in the Maldives.

B. A photo captured an beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives.

C. An photo captured the beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in a Maldives.

D. The photo captured a beautiful sunset. It was captured during our vacation in the Maldives.

options.text: D
options.html: D

options.text: A
options.html: A

options.text: B
options.html: B

options.text: C
options.html: C

questions.solution:
The definite article 'the' should be used before 'photo' and 'Maldives' because in both instances, it introduces specific nouns, that is, 'a particular photo that captured a sunset' and 'a place (Maldives)'.

The indefinite article 'a' should be used before 'beautiful' as it is referring to an unspecified noun, that is, 'sunset'. Since 'beautiful' is not a vowel-sounding word, 'an' cannot be used before it.

The sentences A, B, and C depict grammatically incorrect usage of the articles.

Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

Note:

Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

questions.solution:

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.questionHtml: Select the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: They have know each other since childhood.
options.html: They have know each other since childhood.

options.text: Arnav has lived in this city for ten years.
options.html: Arnav has lived in this city for ten years.

options.text: We have just move into our new house.
options.html: We have just move into our new house.

options.text: They had buy tickets for the concert, but it was cancelled at the last minute.
options.html: They had buy tickets for the concert, but it was cancelled at the last minute.

questions.solution:
The sentence given in option (b) is grammatically correct.

Option (a) is not correct. In the present perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'have'), the correct form of the main verb after "have" is the past participle form. But 'know' (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'know' should be replaced with the past participle form 'known'. The correct sentence is: They have known each other since childhood.

Option (c) is incorrect. In the present perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'have'), the correct form of the main verb after "have" is the past participle form. But 'move' (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'move' should be replaced with the past participle form 'moved'. The correct sentence is: We have just moved into our new house.

Option (d) is also incorrect. In the past perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'had'), the correct form of the main verb after "had" is the past participle form. But the verb "buy" (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'buy' should be replaced with the past participle form 'bought'. Also, "had bought" is used to indicate an action that occurred before another action in the past (in this case, the cancellation of the concert).

The correct sentence is: They had bought tickets for the concert, but it was cancelled at the last minute. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

questions.question: Select the option that expresses the following sentence in superlative degree of comparison. He is a fast runner.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in superlative degree of comparison.

He is a fast runner.

options.text: He is the fastest runner.
options.html: He is the fastest runner.

options.text: He is faster than any runner.
options.html: He is faster than any runner.

options.text: No other runner is as faster as he is.
options.html: No other runner is as faster as he is.

options.text: No change required.
options.html: No change required.

questions.solution:
The adjective is 'fast' and it is in the positive degree, which means it does not show any comparison. To change a sentence from the positive degree to the superlative degree, we need to add -est to the adjective and use the definite article 'the' before it. The superlative degree shows that something or someone has the highest degree of quality among all the others in a group.

Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

Option (b) is in comparative degree.

Option (c) is incorrect as 'faster' is in the comparative degree while the positive degree is used with 'as...as'.

Note:

Adjectives: Words which are used with a noun/pronoun to describe or point out, the person, animal, place, or thing which the noun names, or to tell the number or quantity, are called Adjectives.

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

Note:

Definite and indefinite articles: In the English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.

II. We're going to a party.

· The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take a position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition.

· The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.
